description: Hey I'm Nila, I'm interested in exploring space and quite a fanatic about the physics and mathematics behind it.
summary:
In aerospace engineering, space exploration is never a conquest of unlimited power—it is a fragile state of debt. Every ounce of propellant, every kilowatt of solar energy, and every minute in a planetary shadow is on borrowed time and borrowed physics.

BORROWED is an authentic, interactive space mission architecture and spacecraft systems simulator developed by Team ESKIMOS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge under the "Space Mission Design Game" track.

Stepping into the role of a NASA Mission Architect, players design, assemble, verify, and launch probes to Low Earth Orbit (Earth observation radar), the Lunar South Pole (Artemis water-ice reconnaissance), Mars (interplanetary cruise & surface descent), and Saturn (via a high-velocity Jupiter gravity assist). Every design is audited in real time against the multi-stage Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Barrowman aerodynamic stability (CP vs. CG), US Standard Atmosphere 1976 Max-Q dynamic pressure, solar inverse-square decay, eclipse battery reserves, and NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) link budgets.

Featuring a live CAD schematic visualizer, custom 3D orbital trajectory rendering, and NASA DONKI space weather events, BORROWED bridges rigorous aerospace systems engineering with accessible gamified education—with zero dependencies.
details:
PROJECT ESKIMOS is an interactive aerospace systems engineering simulator that places players in the role of a NASA Mission Architect responsible for leading a spacecraft design review. The simulator allows players to experience the complete process of designing, assembling, evaluating, and launching spacecraft using realistic aerospace engineering principles. It begins with mission selection, offering four NASA-inspired flight scenarios: Low Earth Orbit missions involving NISAR and Landsat radar, Lunar South Pole exploration based on the Artemis VIPER water-ice detection mission, Mars interplanetary transfers inspired by Perseverance and MAVEN, and a Jupiter gravity-assist trajectory towards Saturn inspired by Voyager and Cassini. Players then proceed to spacecraft and launch vehicle assembly, where they configure aerodynamic nose cones such as von Kármán, Sears-Haack, ogive, and conical designs; select airframe materials including CFRP, Al-Li 2195, and Stainless Steel 301; and assemble fins, multistage propulsion systems, power arrays, batteries, deep-space antennas, and scientific payloads. Available propulsion technologies include Hydrolox, Methalox, Kerolox, solid rocket motors, and NASA NEXT ion engines. Before launch clearance is granted, the simulator performs a real-time systems audit to evaluate essential engineering constraints, including mass margins of at least 15%, delta-v reserves of at least 10%, Barrowman aerodynamic static stability through the relationship between the centre of pressure and centre of gravity, solar flux variation according to the inverse-square law, and battery capacity during orbital eclipses. Once the spacecraft passes the required checks, players can launch their missions in a 3D orbital simulation environment featuring stage separation, Hohmann transfer trajectories, and real-time NASA DONKI space-weather hazards.

PROJECT ESKIMOS aims to make aerospace systems engineering more accessible by transforming complex textbook equations into interactive visual representations and colour-coded engineering margin indicators. It introduces players to the importance of engineering trade-offs, demonstrating how adding scientific instruments increases spacecraft mass, which subsequently increases power requirements, demands larger solar arrays, and ultimately affects propulsion and fuel requirements. The simulator also promotes universal accessibility by operating directly within modern web browsers without requiring software installations, compilers, external frameworks, or backend servers. Its primary objective is to inspire and educate the next generation of aerospace engineers, students, and space enthusiasts. By releasing PROJECT ESKIMOS as free, open-source software under the MIT License, the project aims to provide high school astronomy clubs, university engineering classes, and public science museums with an interactive educational platform for understanding orbital mechanics, spacecraft design, and mission planning.

The project is developed using pure Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript (ES6+), without relying on external frameworks, npm packages, Python, or Node.js runtime requirements. Its visualisation capabilities are supported by custom HTML5 Canvas-based rendering engines, including an orbital trajectory visualiser implemented in orbitView.js and a real-time CAD rocket blueprint generator implemented in rocketView.js. The project also incorporates the Web Audio API to generate procedural audio effects, including launch tones, countdown sequences, and thruster sounds, without requiring external audio files. This lightweight architecture ensures that the simulator remains accessible and can operate efficiently across different devices and platforms.

One of the project's most creative features is its live CAD blueprint visualiser, which dynamically generates aerospace schematics as players modify spacecraft components such as nose cones, fuel tanks, fins, and engines. It also displays the centre of gravity (Xcg) and centre of pressure (Xcp) vectors to help players understand aerodynamic stability. When the stability margin falls below 0.5 calibres, the simulation introduces dynamic rocket tumbling during the maximum dynamic pressure phase (Max-Q). Another innovative feature is the integration of dynamic space-weather hazards during interplanetary missions, where coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and solar proton events based on NASA DONKI data challenge players to consider radiation protection and spacecraft reliability. These engineering-focused features are complemented by procedural interstellar nebulae, animated starfields, and atmospheric condensation shock cones, creating an engaging visual experience while maintaining the project's technical focus.

The development of PROJECT ESKIMOS considers several important engineering and mission-planning factors. Its technical foundation draws upon the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (SP-2016-6105 Rev 2) and NASA SP-8000 launch vehicle sizing standards. Astrodynamics and trajectory simulations incorporate Walter Hohmann transfer orbits, patched-conic hyperbolic gravity assists, and a Jupiter gravity-assist scenario involving an approximate velocity change of +9,200 m/s. Atmospheric calculations use the US Standard Atmosphere 1976 model to represent dynamic pressure and maximum aerodynamic loading during launch. The simulator also incorporates Deep Space Network (DSN) free-space path loss (FSPL) calculations to evaluate telecommunications link budgets. In addition to technical performance, financial constraints and mission risks are considered through budget ceilings and mass-margin requirements, encouraging players to optimise spacecraft efficiency rather than simply selecting the most expensive components. Overall, PROJECT ESKIMOS combines aerospace engineering, interactive simulation, and educational game design to create an accessible platform for exploring the complexities of real-world space mission development.PROJECT ESKIMOS is an interactive aerospace systems engineering simulator that places players in the role of a NASA Mission Architect responsible for leading a spacecraft design review.
